Melanoblast migration through the epidermis: A newly defined e-cadherin mechanism and its relevance to Pigmentary disorders and melanoma

Denay JK Richards, and Danelle Devenport DOI: https://www.doi.org/10.22271/allresearch.2026.v12.i9a.14063 Abstract Melanocytes originate outside the skin and must travel as precursor cells, called melanoblasts, through the tightly interconnected layers of the epidermis before they can populate the hair follicles and skin surface. How melanoblasts cross keratinocyte layers without breaching the epidermal barrier has been unclear. Using high-resolution live imaging and conditional knockout mice, Richards and colleagues recently showed that murine melanoblasts form extensive, but atypical, E-cadherin–based attachments to surrounding keratinocytes as they migrate through both the basal and suprabasal layers of the epidermis. Unlike the classic, catenin-anchored E-cadherin junctions that lock neighboring keratinocytes together, melanoblast–keratinocyte E-cadherin adhesions are comparatively poor in the cytoplasmic catenins that couple cadherins to the actin cytoskeleton and turn over more rapidly. Deleting E-cadherin from either melanoblasts or keratinocytes destabilized melanoblast protrusions, slowed migration, and produced patchy depigmentation in adult mice. This review summarizes these findings for a clinical dermatology audience and considers their relevance to three areas of clinical interest: patterned congenital pigmentary disorders such as piebaldism, the melanocyte–keratinocyte adhesion defect already described in vitiligo, and the cadherin changes accompanying melanoma invasion. Understanding how normal melanocyte precursors move without disrupting tissue integrity may reframe how pathologic melanocyte detachment, migration, and invasion are conceptualized in skin disease. Keywords: Melanoblast; E-cadherin; melanocyte–keratinocyte adhesion; vitiligo; piebaldism; melanoma invasion; skin pigmentation Introduction Why Melanocyte Positioning Matters Clinically Melanocytes are the only pigment-producing cells in human skin and hair, and the uniformity of their distribution determines normal pigmentation. Clinically important skin disease spans much of what can go wrong with this distribution: patterned congenital leukoderma when melanocytes fail to arrive in the first place, vitiligo when established melanocytes are lost from otherwise normal skin, and melanoma when melanocytic cells escape the normal constraints on their movement altogether. All epidermal melanocytes descend from melanoblasts, precursor cells that delaminate from the neural crest early in development and must travel long distances through the dermis before crossing into the epidermis [1, 4]. Once inside the epidermis, melanoblasts face a second, less appreciated migratory challenge: they must continue moving through stacked layers of keratinocytes that are themselves bound tightly together by adherens junctions, desmosomes, and tight junctions, in order to fully colonize the interfollicular skin surface and hair follicles before birth [1, 4]. Melanoblasts that fail to complete this journey leave behind unpigmented skin, a mechanism already well-established for congenital patterned hypopigmentation such as piebaldism [5]. Separately, in adults, loss of normal melanocyte– keratinocyte adhesion has been implicated in vitiligo, [6]. And a shift away from E-cadherin– based adhesion is a well-described feature of melanoma progression, in which transformed melanocytes escape keratinocyte-imposed growth control and invade the dermis [7, 12]. the basic cell-biological question of how melanoblasts move as individual cells between keratinocytes that are otherwise firmly locked together, without tearing open the epidermal barrier has remained largely unanswered. This question was addressed directly in a mouse study published in the Journal of Cell Biology by Richards and colleagues [1].The findings are summarized below for a clinical audience, followed by a discussion of where this basic biology may intersect with dermatologic disease. What the Study Found Using mouse reporter lines that separately and simultaneously label melanoblasts and keratinocytes with different fluorescent markers, the investigators performed live confocal imaging of intact embryonic skin explants, allowing individual melanoblasts to be tracked in real time as they colonized the epidermis [1]. Melanoblasts were found to migrate through both the deepest (basal) layer of the epidermis, where they contact the basement membrane, and the more superficial (suprabasal) layers, which lack a basement membrane entirely. Individual cells moved back and forth between these compartments and spent a substantial fraction of imaging time in the suprabasal layers, with especially dense accumulation around developing hair follicles. To move, melanoblasts extended multiple branching, finger-like protrusions that gripped onto adjacent keratinocyte surfaces. Quantitative imaging showed that melanoblasts express E-cadherin at levels equal to or exceeding that of surrounding keratinocytes and use it to form direct, extensive contacts with keratinocyte membranes rather than relying solely on the basement membrane as a migratory substrate. The unexpected finding concerned the molecular composition of these contacts. Despite carrying abundant E-cadherin, melanoblast– keratinocyte junctions recruited substantially less of the cytoplasmic catenin proteins (α-catenin, β-catenin, and p120-catenin) that normally couple E-cadherin to the actin cytoskeleton and give keratinocyte–keratinocyte junctions their mechanical strength. Photobleaching experiments showed that E-cadherin at melanoblast–keratinocyte contacts also turns over and is replenished faster than Ecadherin at keratinocyte–keratinocyte junctions consistent with a more dynamic, less mechanically rigid mode of adhesion. To test whether this atypical adhesion was functionally required, the investigators genetically deleted E-cadherin selectively from melanoblasts, and in a separate model, deleted E-Cadherin from keratinocytes using cell type specific Cre recombinase systems. Live-imaging migration assays, performed in the melanoblast-specific (Tyr-Cre) model, showed that melanoblasts formed fewer and less stable protrusions and migrated more slowly and over shorter distances. In fixed-tissue analyses, melanoblasts in both models showed reduced dendritic complexity and were less often found in the suprabasal epidermis. The functional consequence was visible after birth as postnatal mice lacking melanoblast E-cadherin developed patches of unpigmented skin concentrated on the ventral trunk, tail, and distal limbs - the body regions farthest from the melanoblasts' point of origin and therefore the last to be colonized during normal development. Taken together, the data indicate that melanoblasts do not passively slip between

keratinocytes. They actively grip keratinocyte surfaces using an E-cadherin–based adhesion that is molecularly related to, but functionally distinct from the strong junctions keratinocytes use to hold onto one another and that this distinctive, catenin-poor adhesion is required for melanoblasts to fully and directionally populate the skin (Figure 1). Clinical Relevance Patterned Congenital Pigmentary Disorders Piebaldism, caused by loss-of-function mutations in KIT, is classically explained by impaired melanoblast survival, proliferation, and migration from the neural crest, producing a stereotyped pattern of depigmented patches on the central forehead (white forelock), anterior trunk, and extremities, typically sparing the hands, feet, and periorbital and perioral skin [5]. The regional pattern of depigmentation seen in Ecadherin–deficient mice in this study, concentrated ventrally and distally, parallels the topography of human piebaldism and related patterned leukodermas, even though the underlying molecular lesion (an adhesion protein rather than a receptor tyrosine kinase) differs from KIT. (Table 1). This raises the possibility that melanocyte adhesion to the keratinocyte microenvironment is just as important in melanoblast migration as intrinsic melanocyte migratory ability. E-cadherin and catenin pathway genes may be worth considering as candidates in the genetic evaluation of otherwise unexplained congenital patterned hypopigmentation or as an explanation for the extent of depigmentation in congenital piebaldism. Yet, this remains a hypothesis generated by the mouse data rather than a demonstrated human mechanism. Vitiligo Loss of normal melanocyte–keratinocyte adhesion architecture has independently been described in adult vitiligo. In perilesional and lesional vitiligo skin, melanocytes show reduced and mislocalized E-cadherin at their interfaces with keratinocytes, and this adhesion defect has been proposed to precede clinically visible depigmentation [6]. Because the present study shows that melanoblast– keratinocyte E-cadherin is molecularly distinct from ordinary keratinocyte junctions, lower in catenins and more dynamic, the vitiligo-associated loss of E-cadherin may not represent uniform loss of an otherwise stable adhesive "glue," but rather disruption of an already unusual, labile adhesion system that adult melanocytes may continue to depend on for their function and/or survival. If adult melanocytes retain something closer to this developmental, catenin-poor adhesion state, they could be intrinsically more susceptible to detachment-associated cell death or immunemediated destruction than the keratinocytes around them, offering one plausible contributor to why melanocytes, rather than keratinocytes, are selectively lost in vitiligo. (Table 1) This also impacts the clinical approach to repigmentation. Approaches that stabilize or promote this adhesion-dependent migration, rather than targeting only the immune attack on melanocytes, represent an underexplored angle for improving repigmentation outcomes. Melanoma Invasion E-cadherin loss, and a shift toward N-cadherin expression, is among the most consistently described molecular events in melanoma progression, releasing transformed melanocytes from keratinocyte-imposed growth control and adhesion and enabling invasion into the dermis [7-12]. The present findings complicate a simple version of this narrative. Melanoblasts express E-cadherin at levels equal to or higher than neighboring keratinocytes and yet migrate as individual, highly motile cells not because they lack E-cadherin, but because their E-cadherin is functionally uncoupled from the catenin–actin machinery that would otherwise anchor them in place. This suggests an additional route to invasive, single-cell melanocytic behavior that does not require transcriptional loss of E-cadherin: post-translational or trafficking changes that reduce catenin engagement at existing E-cadherin junctions could, in principle, permit single-cell motility while E-cadherin remains detectable by routine immunohistochemistry. This is a useful caution for dermatopathology, where E-cadherin staining is sometimes used as supportive evidence of a well-differentiated, less invasive melanocytic lesion. These data suggest that Ecadherin expression alone does not guarantee intact adhesion, and that catenin engagement at the junction, which is not a routine clinical assay, may better reflect the functional adhesive state of a melanocytic cell. This interpretation assumes that differentiated melanocytes actively upregulate catenin engagement to remain stably anchored in situ, a premise that has not been directly

demonstrated and would be worth testing explicitly in adult tissue. More broadly, if catenin engagement, rather than Ecadherin expression, determines whether a melanocytic cell can move as an individual through tissue, then diagnostic or therapeutic strategies aimed at the cadherin–catenin coupling step, rather than E-cadherin expression level alone, merit further investigation in melanoma biology as they could allow the progress of melanoma invasion and further metastasis. (Table 1) Limitations and What Is Needed to Bridge Mouse Findings to Human Skin These findings derive from mouse embryonic skin explants and genetically engineered mice. Mouse and human epidermis share the same fundamental architecture and melanocyte biology, but direct confirmation in human fetal or adult skin, and in patient-derived tissue from piebaldism, vitiligo, and melanoma, is needed before these mechanisms can be considered established in humans. The developmental window studied, embryonic melanoblast migration, differs from the quiescent adult melanocyte population most relevant to vitiligo and melanoma, although prior work cited within the study suggests adult melanocyte–keratinocyte adhesion continues to depend on E-cadherin. The mouse model used complete, cell type– specific knockouts, a more severe perturbation than the partial reductions in E-cadherin expression or localization typically observed in human disease, so dose-dependent or partial-loss effects remain untested. These diagnostic hypotheses raised above require additional direct genetic and histologic validation before they can inform clinical practice. Yet, it supports the investigation of a previously unexplored connection between intracellular catenin in migratory melanocytic disease in clinical dermatology.

Conclusion Melanoblasts migrate through the epidermis by forming an E-cadherin–based adhesion to keratinocytes that is deliberately weaker and more dynamic than the junctions keratinocytes use to hold onto each other, allowing individual melanocyte precursors to move through tissue without disrupting it. This developmental mechanism offers a coherent framework for thinking about three areas of clinical interest: the anatomic pattern of congenital hypopigmentation in piebaldism, the selective vulnerability of melanocytes in vitiligo, and the possibility that melanoma cells can achieve invasive, single-cell motility through altered catenin engagement rather than E-cadherin loss alone. Exploring the interconnectivity between extracellular cadherins and intracellular catenins in histopathology of dermatologic melanocytic disorders will allow for a better understanding of the molecular mechanisms behind migration and invasion in melanocytic lesions.
